newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr seen range-bound in Asia, high near 126.50 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen range-bound in Asia, high near 126.50 yen.

text.p: The dollar is expected to be range-bound and top-heavy during Asian trading time on Wednesday, weighed down by a combination of continuing concern on possible Bank of Japan (BOJ) dollar-selling intervention and lower-than-expected U.S. consumer price data released Tuesday.
The U.S. Labor Department reported that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent overall in March and 0.2 percent excluding food and energy items.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of 0.2 percent overall and 0.3 percent in the core component.

A trust bank dealer said release of the data had sparked some profit-taking in U.S. trading time, with offers from U.S. funds and securities firms, and Japanese institutional investors, apparently lined up from 126.50-70 yen on up.

These conditions, along with a severe lack of fresh factors, are expected to keep dollar gains capped near 126.50 yen. "But actually upward moves may be even more limited, perhaps to around 126.30 yen," the trust bank dealer added.
Although he said there appeared to be some stop-loss sales lined up under 126 yen, these were light at best, with bargain hunting at the upper end of the 125-126 yen range likely.

The dollar eased against the mark overnight despite comments from Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, who said the launch of the single European currency, or euro, could casue shifts from mark-denominated investments to dollar-denominated ones. Ultimately, the greenback's lack of gains on the yen dragged the dollar down against the mark as well.

The market will be waiting for possible comments from Eisuke Sakakibara at a gathering of Japanese foreign exchange traders starting at 6.30 p.m. (0930 GMT). "We may well get some yen-positive statements from him," one dealer said.
But dealers said even this sort of comment was unlikely to take the dollar down much, as a lack of long positions accumulated in the market makes sudden downward moves more unlikely.
